lesson_title: One Hub, Nine Eggs and a Rugby Pass: Chemistry Exam Essentials
hook_text: 4 cups of flour, 9 eggs, recipe says 1 cup + 3 eggs per batch. Everyone counts the flour. Chemistry counts the eggs.
clip_script: The recipe: one cup of flour and three eggs make ten pancakes. Your shelf: four cups of flour and nine eggs. Instinct glances at the four generous cups of flour and relaxes. But run the demand check: four cups of flour demand twelve eggs, and the shelf holds nine. The eggs run out first: the EGGS are the limiting ingredient, the flour is in excess, and the kitchen makes exactly three batches — thirty pancakes — with a full cup of flour abandoned on the shelf, useless without partners. That demand-versus-supply check is the complete limiting-reagent method.
visual_style: A kitchen counter with flour cups and eggs stacked as tally bars; demand arrows reaching from each cup toward the eggs it needs and snapping short at nine; the spare flour cup greying out as thirty pancakes stack; the counter dissolving into a balanced equation with moles replacing cups and eggs.
mood: Kitchen game-show energy — a feared exam topic revealed as breakfast arithmetic.
pacing: Quick shelf reveal, the wrong instinct dangled, the demand check as the twist, pancake payoff and the chemistry morph.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision lesson and cross every stoichiometry bridge without a wobble.
